A month with no shipments at all stays in the series as a zero and remains visible, whereas a groupby on the date string would simply not produce that row, and a gap in shipments would look like the absence of a gap.

traps.message: The column holds a rolling sum, not a rolling average: the values are three times the level of the series, and a monthly spike is invisible against them. After .rolling(3) the aggregating function is .mean(), not .sum(): the window itself computes nothing.

tasks.title: A spike against its level
tasks.brief: Your manager looks at the monthly series and argues with himself: is the autumn of 2025 a spike, or ordinary swings of the kind this series has plenty of?
tasks.goal: Add a rolling3 column to the monthly series of Setouchi shipments: the rolling mean of units over the last three months.
hints: The window is set in observations: rolling(3) means the last three months of the series, current month included.
rolling(3) only defines the window; the value is computed by the function after it, .mean().
tasks.explain: The rolling mean is here not to remove the spike but to make visible the level it stands against. The window is deliberately shorter than the phenomenon: the spike lasts three months, and a three-month window rises along with it while still not dissolving it into two years of ordinary work, which is what a yearly window would do. The general rule: a smoothing window is chosen to match the scale of what you want to see, not the smoothness of the line.

tasks.title: The flow is back, and the stock?
tasks.brief: By January 2026 «Setouchi Trading» shipments were back to ordinary numbers, and the sales department considers the question closed.
tasks.goal: Tell a flow from a stock: work out what the inventory series shows once shipments have normalized.
tasks.predictQuestion: Since January 2026 Setouchi shipments have held at the usual 3.5 to 6 thousand units a month, the same as before the autumn. What will the inventory series at their warehouse show for the last ten months?

options.label: Stock grew almost fivefold over the three months of the spike and has held around 21 to 22 thousand units ever since, with no decline
options.why: Shipments are a flow, inventory is a level, and normalizing the first does not by itself touch the second. The goods brought in last autumn have not gone anywhere: they sit there, and the outlets sell them at exactly the same rate as before.

options.label: Stock returned to the earlier 4 thousand units along with shipments: once the flow normalized, the inventory cleared
options.why: That is what would happen if sales had grown and absorbed what was brought in. But sell-out at Setouchi outlets did not grow in the autumn, it dipped, and has run at the usual level since. There is nothing to clear the stock with.

options.label: Stock declines steadily from December: the goods are selling through, just more slowly than usual
options.why: A steady decline would mean sales exceed purchases. But shipments came back to the level of sales, not below it, so the stock is not being drawn down. It is standing still.

options.label: Stock jumps from month to month, so nothing can be said from such a series
options.why: It is the flow that jumps, not the level. Warehouse stock is a cumulative quantity and changes only by the difference between what came in and what went out, which makes its series smooth by nature.

hints: A shipment is how much arrived during the month. Stock is how much is lying there at the end of it. The first can return to normal without changing the second.
Look at the two ends of the series rather than its shape: compare the last value with what it was before the autumn.
tasks.explain: This is the difference between a flow and a stock, and it is also why the sell-in to sell-out ratio answers only half the question. The ratio is back to 1.05, meaning the partner again buys exactly what it sells, yet the roughly 22 thousand units brought in beyond demand last autumn are still sitting there. Until they are sold, the next orders will be either smaller than usual or absent altogether, which for us means that any plan for this distributor over the coming quarters is built on sand. «Has the flow returned?» and «are the consequences exhausted?» are different questions, and the second one is read off the level, not the flow.

tasks.title: A date that stayed text
tasks.brief: A colleague built a weekly sales series for «Aqualis» and wants to roll it up into months for a meeting. The week_start column became the index but was never converted to a date.
tasks.goal: Understand why resample needs an index of real dates, not text that looks like dates.
tasks.predictQuestion: The week_start column came from the database as text like '2024-01-01', and the colleague skipped converting it: «you can see they're dates anyway». What will the last line do?

options.label: It fails with a TypeError: resample only works with an index of dates, and this index is text
options.why: To a person '2024-01-01' is a date; to pandas it's a string, and the index is whatever the column was when it came from the database. resample needs a calendar, where a month ends and which weeks fall into it, and text has no calendar. So the error is loud and on its own line, and the fix is one line: pd.to_datetime(...) before set_index.

options.label: It returns a monthly series: pandas recognizes dates in strings like 2024-01-01 on its own
options.why: pandas can recognize dates in text, but only when asked: pd.to_datetime, or parse_dates when reading. set_index doesn't change the column's type; the index stays the same text the column was.

options.label: It adds up the weeks by the first seven characters of the date, which means by month
options.why: resample doesn't cut strings or look at characters. Grouping by a .str[:7] slice would have to be written by hand, and that's exactly the workaround that breaks on the first quarter or rolling window: text dates don't contain them.

options.label: It returns the same weekly series: since the frequency can't change, pandas leaves it alone
options.why: resample can't decline quietly: if there's nothing to change the frequency from, it doesn't hand back the original, it fails. That's good news: weeks silently returned instead of months would only get noticed in the meeting.

hints: Follow the type of week_start from reading the table to set_index: nothing along the way changes it.
resample sorts observations into calendar months. Does text have a calendar?
tasks.explain: This is a convenient error: it fails immediately, on the line where the mistake is. That's why preparing a series takes two steps: pd.to_datetime turns text into a date, set_index makes it the axis, and only then does resample know where a month ends. The order matters: set_index without to_datetime still gives you an index, just a text one, exactly as here. The third call often written next to them, sort_index, doesn't prevent this error and isn't needed by resample, which sorts observations into months itself. Sorting matters for operations that take neighbors in row order, rolling for example.

tasks.title: Setouchi's October, row by row
tasks.brief: Before computing anything about «Setouchi Trading», your manager wants a look at the raw rows for one month: what October 2025 looks like in the shipment table.
tasks.goal: Return product_id and units from fact_sellin for distributor 1 with month_start = '2025-10-01'.
hints: There are two conditions, one on distributor_id and one on month_start, each in its own brackets with & between them.
month_start is stored as text, so it is compared with a quoted string: '2025-10-01'.
tasks.explain: 44 rows, one per product Setouchi ordered in October, 10,172 units in total. A list like that cannot be read by eye: a row talks about a product, while the question is about the month as a whole. Hence the next step, collapsing the rows by grouping. Notice also that month_start is text here, not a date: comparing it with '2025-10-01' works because the characters match, not because pandas understands months.

traps.message: Months after December got into the sum: the condition sets only the start of the period, and the data runs to June 2026. That is why every distributor shows several times more units than one quarter holds.

October is missing: the strict comparison > '2025-10-01' drops the first month of the quarter, because month_start holds the first day of the month. That is why every distributor shows about a third fewer units.

tasks.title: Shipments by distributor for Q4
tasks.brief: Finance wants total shipments per distributor for October to December 2025. The table will be compared with others later, so the distributor has to be an ordinary column rather than sit in the index.
tasks.goal: From the fact_sellin rows for the three months of Q4 2025, return distributor_id and units, the total number of units for each distributor, with distributor_id as an ordinary column.
hints: Three links in one chain: group by distributor_id, pick units, collapse with a sum.
After grouping the key moves into the index. To bring it back as a column, end the chain with .reset_index().
tasks.explain: Setouchi has 28,203 units for the quarter; the next one, Hokusei Trading, has 12,018. The total on its own proves nothing yet: a large distributor is supposed to take more. Whether this is a lot is decided by a comparison, with the same quarter a year earlier or with sales at its outlets, and both need distributor_id as a column, because that is what the table is later joined and filtered on. as_index=False inside groupby would give the same result: it is the other way to keep the key out of the index.

tasks.title: The same quarter a year earlier
tasks.brief: In Q4 2025, Setouchi Trading took 28,203 units. Whether that's a lot or a little needs a reference point. The fairest one is the same quarter a year earlier: the same season, the same partner.
tasks.goal: From the fact_sellin rows for October to December 2024, return distributor_id and units, the total number of units for each distributor, with distributor_id as an ordinary column.
hints: The chain is the same as for Q4 2025: groupby on distributor_id, units, sum.
For the key as a column, end the chain with .reset_index().
tasks.explain: A year earlier Setouchi took 13,341 units: first place, but only 475 units ahead of Hokusei Trading (12,866). In 2025 every one of the other eleven came in 3 to 14% below its previous autumn quarter, while Setouchi doubled. Comparing a partner with itself a year earlier is the cheapest test of whether something is normal: it removes both the season and the size of the partner, because both are the same.

tasks.title: Setouchi shipments month by month
tasks.brief: The distributor KAM is sure the autumn spike at Setouchi Trading was a one-off. The only way to check is across the full length: what an ordinary month looks like for this partner and how many months broke out of it.
tasks.goal: From the fact_sellin rows for distributor 1, return month_start and units, the total units for each month, with month_start as an ordinary column.
hints: Group by month_start: one row of the result is one month.
as_index=False inside groupby keeps month_start a column.
tasks.explain: Thirty months, and an ordinary Setouchi month runs from 3,575 to 6,646 units. Three in a row break out: October, November and December 2025, at 10,172, 8,162 and 9,869. That is not one odd month but a quarter, and from January shipments are back within the usual range. The grouping here runs on text, which works as long as every month has at least one row: a month with no shipments at all would simply not appear in such a table. Setouchi has no such months, but a time series should not carry that weakness.

traps.message: The units column shows the same numbers as orders: the units were counted, not added up. count answers "how many rows", not "how many units are in those rows".

tasks.title: More rows or more units
tasks.brief: The first question about a spike in shipments is whether it is an export error. A duplicated load is easy to spot in the table: twice as many rows, with the same quantity in each.
tasks.goal: From the fact_sellin rows for distributor 1, return two measures for each month_start: orders, the number of rows (count over sellin_id), and units, the total number of units.
hints: Named aggregation: name=('column', 'function'). Rows are counted with count over a column that has no gaps, sellin_id for example.
Units are added up: the function is 'sum'.
tasks.explain: Setouchi always has between 38 and 44 rows a month, one per product ordered, and October to December 2025 have 44, 44 and 42, like any other month. They are the same 44 products as across the whole history, and none appears twice in a month. What grew is not the number of rows but the units in each: 10,172 in October against 6,019 in September on the same 44 rows. A duplicated load would show the opposite picture. So these are real orders: the usual products, taken with a margin.

tasks.title: Did the outlets sell more
tasks.brief: If demand at Setouchi grew in the autumn, shipments simply followed it and the spike is explained by sales. The check runs through the outlets it serves: their sales sit in fact_sellout, and the link to the distributor is in dim_customer.
tasks.goal: Work out what sales at Setouchi outlets did in the quarter of the spike.
tasks.predictQuestion: Setouchi shipments in Q4 2025 were 28,203 units against 13,341 a year earlier. What will q4_2024 and q4_2025, sales at its outlets for the same quarters, show?

options.label: Sales doubled along with shipments: the outlets sold as much as they received
options.why: Then the ratio of shipments to sales would have stayed around one, as it did for the other eleven. For Setouchi it is 2.44, so sales did not follow shipments.

options.label: Sales did not grow, they dipped slightly: 12,673 units in Q4 2024 and 11,574 in Q4 2025
options.why: No demand stood behind the spike: the outlets sold about a thousand units fewer than a year earlier. The goods went to the partner and stayed there, which is where 2.44 comes from: 28,203 shipped against 11,574 sold.

options.label: Sales grew, but less than shipments, by about a third
options.why: Sales growth of even a third would have been visible at the outlets themselves. The data shows none: sales for the quarter are below the previous year, not above it.

options.label: They cannot be compared: sales and distributors live in different tables
options.why: The tables are linked through the outlet: served_by_distributor_id in dim_customer says who serves it. The first line of the code collects those outlets, the second keeps only their sales, and after that it is an ordinary mask on dates.

hints: The first line collects the outlets of the distributor from the reference table, the second keeps only their sales.
Compare with shipments: if sales had doubled, the ratio would have stayed around one.
tasks.explain: Setouchi outlets sold 11,574 units in Q4 2025, 1,099 fewer than a year earlier. Shipments did not follow demand, they went past it. Notice how the selection is built: first the list of outlets from the reference table, then an .isin mask on that list. Sales do not know their distributor; the outlet does, and the road from one to the other runs through the reference table.

tasks.title: Setouchi outlet sales by month
tasks.brief: A monthly shipment series for «Setouchi Trading» is needed next to sales at its outlets, but those sales are stored by week. To put them side by side, the sales need to be brought to the same monthly frequency.
tasks.goal: Collect sales at the outlets of distributor 1 into a monthly series of units with resample.
hints: resample changes the frequency; month start is written 'MS'.
The index is already prepared: the date has been converted from text and set as the axis.
tasks.explain: Sales at Setouchi outlets in October, November and December 2025 were 4,064, 3,379 and 4,131 units, 11,574 for the quarter against 12,673 a year earlier. Shipments in the same months were 10,172, 8,162 and 9,869. Two series at the same frequency can now be laid side by side. resample over weekly dates assigns a week to the month it starts in: the week of 29 September lands in September, although almost all of it lies in October. There is no need to change that rule; what matters is that both series you are going to compare are counted by the same one.

tasks.title: 2.44 in pandas
tasks.brief: The ratio of shipments to sales for each distributor in Q4 2025 needs to be assembled so that recomputing it for any other period is a single edit, not a new query: two facts, each collapsed to one row per distributor, then joined.
tasks.goal: For each distributor in Q4 2025, return distributor_id, shipped (units shipped), sold (units sold at its outlets in the weeks starting in October to December) and ratio (shipped / sold, rounded to two decimal places).
hints: The first join attaches each sale to the distributor of its outlet: the key is customer_id, and it is unique on the right.
The second joins the two collapsed tables on a shared column, the one outlets was renamed for.
tasks.explain: The same table as the query gave: Setouchi at 28,203 against 11,574, which is 2.44, the other eleven at 1.04 to 1.05. It is built the same way as the query with two WITH blocks: each fact is first collapsed to one row per distributor, and only then are the collapsed tables joined. The first merge attaches its outlet to each sale; customer_id is unique on the right, hence validate='many_to_one'. The second joins the two collapsed tables on distributor_id, where the key is unique on both sides. The column in outlets is renamed exactly for that second join: merge with on= looks for a column with the same name in both tables.

tasks.title: The ratio for Q1 2026
tasks.brief: The distributor KAM says that since January Setouchi has been buying as usual. Checking that means recomputing the same shipments-to-sales ratio, but for Q1 2026: the period changes, the method stays the same.
tasks.goal: For Q1 2026, return distributor_id, shipped, sold and ratio (shipped / sold, rounded to two decimal places) for each distributor. The collapsed shipped and sold tables are already built in the starter: join them and add ratio.
hints: The two collapsed tables join on distributor_id, which is present in both and unique in each.
ratio is a new column: result['ratio'] = (...).round(2).
tasks.explain: In Q1 2026 Setouchi is back in line: 13,432 shipped against 12,717 sold, 1.06, with the others between 1.02 and 1.05. By the yardstick the spike was found with, it is over. The yardstick is fair but narrow: the ratio compares how much came to the partner and how much left it within the same period, two flows. About what piled up between them earlier it says nothing at all.

tasks.title: How many months the stock will last
tasks.brief: The ratio is back to one, while more than twenty thousand units sit in the «Setouchi Trading» warehouse. Sales need a number that translates into a plan: how many months of sales the stock already lying at the partner will cover.
tasks.goal: For each distributor, return distributor_id, stock (units on hand at the end of June 2026), sold (sales at its outlets for the weeks of January to June 2026) and months (how many months of such sales the stock covers: stock / (sold / 6), rounded to one decimal place). stock and sold are already built in the starter.
hints: Stock and sales join on distributor_id, just like shipments and sales in the ratio.
Half a year of sales divided by 6 gives sales per month; divide the stock by that.
tasks.explain: Setouchi holds 22,176 units against outlet sales of about 4,335 a month, which is 5.1 months of stock. The other eleven hold between 1.1 and 1.4 months: as much as it takes to keep the shelf from emptying between deliveries. The difference of four months of sales is what the autumn left behind, and since January it has not shrunk, it has even grown a little: the partner orders exactly as much as it sells. It can clear in one of two ways, the partner skipping orders at some point or the goods reaching their expiry date in the warehouse, and both belong in the plan rather than turning up in it as a surprise.

tasks.title: Two brands over a hundred
tasks.brief: The summer catalogue only takes drinks from the «Aqualis» and «Fruvia» brands, and only items priced above 100 ¥: cheap ones don't go on promo.
tasks.goal: Return sku_code, product_name, brand, list_price for products of the «Aqualis» and «Fruvia» brands priced strictly above 100.
hints: Between .isin([...]) and the next condition pandas expects & (an ampersand), not and: and doesn't work on a column of thousands of values.
The second condition, in its own parentheses, is an ordinary price filter: dim_product['list_price'] > 100.
tasks.explain: .isin(['Aqualis', 'Fruvia']) is pandas's analogue of SQL's IN, and it's already sitting in the template. What's left by hand is the second condition and the connector between them: & evaluates logic element by element across the whole column at once, the only working option for a pandas filter, since and expects a single True/False but gets a Series of thousands instead. The parentheses around each condition aren't decoration: & binds tighter than >, and without them the expression would group in the wrong order.

tasks.title: Quarterly rollup by distributor
tasks.brief: Finance wants total shipments per distributor for October–December 2025. The table will later be compared with others, so the distributor needs to stay a regular column, not the index.
tasks.goal: From fact_sellin for the three months of Q4 2025, return distributor_id and units (the sum of units per distributor). distributor_id as a regular column.
hints: The sum is already there at the end of the chain; what's missing is the grouping before it: q4.groupby('distributor_id').
After grouping the key moves into the index; bring it back as a column with .reset_index() as the last link in the chain.
tasks.explain: Setouchi ships 28,203 units for the quarter, the next distributor, Hokusei Trading, ships 12,018. The sum alone proves nothing yet: a bigger distributor is supposed to take more. Whether it's a lot or a little is decided by comparison, with the same quarter a year earlier or with that distributor's own outlet sales, and both need distributor_id as a column to join and filter on later. as_index=False inside groupby would give the same result: a second way to keep the key out of the index.

tasks.title: Setouchi's discount by month
tasks.brief: The distributor KAM says Setouchi was offered a discount in the autumn to take more stock, "we offered it ourselves." If a discount was offered, it should show up in the shipments, not just in words.
tasks.goal: For distributor Setouchi (distributor_id = 1), return per month: month_start and discount_amount (the sum of discount given).
hints: Selecting one distributor is the same mask as in the quarterly rollup by distributor: distributor_id == 1.
From there it's a familiar chain: group by month, sum the discount, bring the key back as a column: .groupby(...)['...'].sum().reset_index().
tasks.explain: The discount rose to 76,568 / 61,273 / 76,233 ¥ in October–December 2025, nearly double the usual 21,967–47,358 ¥. But units for those same months (the same quarterly rollup by distributor) also rose, 10,172 / 8,162 / 9,869 against 3,764–5,832 a year earlier, and the discount per unit didn't change: 7.5 ¥, same as any other month. The rise in the total is fully explained by the rise in volume, not by more generous terms: there was no volume discount, and Setouchi paid for the extra quarter itself, 2.29 million ¥ against 1.10 million a year before.

tasks.title: Five months of what
tasks.brief: The distributor KAM goes to Setouchi Trading with five months of stock: one number for the whole warehouse. The plan gets recalculated by brand, and a warehouse-wide average can hide very different situations.
tasks.goal: Per brand, return brand, units_on_hand (Setouchi's stock at the end of June 2026), units (sales through its outlets since 2026-01-01), and months (how many months of such sales the stock covers: units_on_hand / (units / 6), rounded to one decimal place).
hints: Stock by brand and sales by brand are two separate calculations: a mask on the distributor, a merge for the brand key, then grouping and summing with .reset_index(), the same sequence of steps as computing stock for the whole warehouse.

Once both tables are rolled up by brand, an ordinary merge on brand joins them; months of stock uses the same yardstick as for the whole warehouse: stock divided by sales per month (six-month sales divided by 6).
tasks.explain: Eight brands hold between 3.8 and 7.7 months of stock; the warehouse-wide "five months" was an average across these eight plus the ninth, Nettora. The ninth, Nettora, sits at 1,368 units against 8 sold in six months, which is 1,026 months: not a duration, a "never." Of the five Setouchi outlets that bought Nettora in 2025, four are among the forty-two the brand lost from January 2026. The average "five months" was hiding two different problems: eight brands can afford to hold off ordering for a few months, and Nettora's stock won't be resolved by recalculating the plan: it needs moving to where the brand still sells.

tasks.title: Price with tax in one line
tasks.brief: The price list needs a table with the price including tax, but the dim_product reference has to stay as it is: other calculations expect it without new columns.
tasks.goal: Build a result table from dim_product with a new column price_with_tax = list_price * 1.1 (a 10% tax, taken as an example), without changing dim_product itself.
hints: assign(name=value) returns a new table with the column added and leaves the original alone.
The new column name is passed as a keyword argument, without quotes: price_with_tax=... .
tasks.explain: assign does not change dim_product: it returns a new table that has everything from before plus the price_with_tax column. That is why it can sit in a chain: each next step gets the result of the previous one. Writing dim_product["price_with_tax"] = ... would do the same, but inside the reference itself, and everyone who reads dim_product afterwards would see the column. The difference between "added to my copy" and "added for everyone" is worked through in the tasks further down the chain.

tasks.title: A "backup copy" of the reference
tasks.brief: An analyst makes a "backup copy" of the product reference by assignment, adds a column to it and is surprised: the column showed up in the original too.
tasks.goal: Understand what the assignment backup = dim_product does: copies the table or gives it a second name.
tasks.predictQuestion: After these two lines: will the archived column appear in dim_product itself?

options.label: Yes, backup and dim_product are two names for the same table in memory, so the column is visible under both
options.why: Assignment in Python does not copy an object, it binds one more name to it. Adding a column changes the object itself, not the name, so the change is visible through either name.

options.label: No, backup got its own data at the moment of assignment, and edits to it do not touch the original
options.why: Only an explicit .copy() gives its own data. Assignment creates no copies, which is why a "backup copy" without .copy() is not a copy at all.

options.label: No, pandas raises an error: a column cannot be added to a table that already has a second name
options.why: There will be no error: pandas does not know about the second name and cannot object. It is the silent change to the original that makes this bug dangerous.

options.label: Yes, but only on big tables; on small ones pandas copies the data itself
options.why: Table size decides nothing. Copying happens only on an explicit .copy(), the same on the 47 rows of dim_product as on the 118 thousand of fact_sellout.

hints: In Python, a = b does not create a new object: both names point to the same one.
How would the same pair of lines end if the first were backup = dim_product.copy()?
tasks.explain: backup = dim_product gives the table a second name, not a copy, so backup["archived"] = True changes the one table that is visible under two names. A real copy is dim_product.copy(): a new object with its own data, and a column added to it leaves the original alone. The same .copy() goes after a filter before writing into a slice, for the same reason: it is needed wherever independence from the source table is needed.

tasks.title: Discount share without a loop
tasks.brief: An analyst computes the discount share in every incoming-shipment row with a loop over rows, and in the browser on 15 thousand rows it noticeably hangs. The same share comes out of one line over the whole column.
tasks.goal: Add a discount_share column to fact_sellin, discount_amount / gross_amount, for all rows at once, with no loop and no apply.
hints: Dividing one column by another works element by element: row by row, with pandas taking care of the loop.
The denominator is the column with the amount before the discount.
tasks.explain: Arithmetic between columns runs for all 15,362 rows of fact_sellin at once in optimized code, instead of a Python call per row. For this task the vectorized form is both shorter and faster, and when a branch on a condition is needed, np.where comes in, as in the neighboring task. The discount share in the dataset lies between 3 and 14 percent; describe() on the new column is enough to see its spread.

tasks.title: Price per pack unit
tasks.brief: A buyer compares prices per pack unit: list_price divided by pack_size. An intern writes it with apply(lambda row: ..., axis=1). Prices can only be compared within one unit of measure (grams with grams, milliliters with milliliters), so the unit column has to be looked at separately.
tasks.goal: Return columns product_id and price_per_unit, where price_per_unit is list_price / pack_size, rounded to 2 places, without apply.
hints: Columns divide by each other element by element, like numbers; the result stays a column of the same length.
A column has its own .round(2), applied to all values at once.
tasks.explain: Dividing list_price by pack_size and rounding are two vectorized operations in a row: neither needs a loop over rows. apply(..., axis=1) would make 47 calls on dim_product and 118,449 on fact_sellout; for a price per unit the difference is harmless, the habit is what hurts: a solution that works on a reference quietly becomes slow on facts. price_per_unit can only be compared within one unit, so the next step of such an analysis is grouping by unit.

tasks.title: The brand's average price next to each product
tasks.brief: A category manager needs a product reference where each product's price has its brand's average price beside it, so it is visible at once who costs more than their own. A separate brand summary table is not needed: the row count should stay equal to the number of products.
tasks.goal: Add a brand_avg_price column to dim_product, the average list_price of this product's brand, on each of the 47 rows.
hints: agg("mean") would collapse 47 rows to one per brand, and one row per product is needed.
The method that returns a group's value at the original granularity is the same one that computes a row's share of its group total.
tasks.explain: transform("mean") computes the mean for each group and spreads it back across the rows of the original table, so the row count does not change (47) and the column sits beside the price without a join. In SQL this is AVG(list_price) OVER (PARTITION BY brand): a window function instead of a collapsing group. On such a column one comparison finds a product pricier than its brand: list_price > brand_avg_price.

traps.message: One average over the whole table (230.34) was subtracted, not the average of the product's own category. As a result almost every Beverages product looks "cheap" and every OTC product "pricey": the gap shows the category, not the product's place inside it. The mean has to be computed within groups: groupby("category") and transform("mean").

tasks.title: Pricier or cheaper than its category
tasks.brief: Prices from different categories cannot be compared directly: an average Beverages product costs about 95, an average OTC product about 423. The buyer needs to know how much each product is above or below its own category's average price.
tasks.goal: Add a price_gap column to dim_product: list_price minus the mean list_price of this product's category, rounded to 2 places.
hints: The category average is needed on each product row: a column as long as the table, which is groupby plus transform, not agg.
The gap is a plain subtraction of two columns; round at the very end with a single .round(2).
tasks.explain: transform("mean") brings the category average price onto each product row, and subtraction gives the gap: a product at 150 in Beverages is pricey (average 95.33), while a product at 150 in OTC is cheap (average 423.17). Within each category the gaps sum to zero up to rounding, which is how to check the average was computed over the same rows. In SQL: list_price - AVG(list_price) OVER (PARTITION BY category).

traps.message: The cells hold product numbers added up instead of counted: Beverages in FMCG shows 78 instead of 12, OTC in Pharma 693 instead of 18. A sum of identifiers means nothing, because product_id is a label, not a quantity. To find how many products there are, count them: aggfunc="count".

tasks.title: Assortment: categories by division
tasks.brief: The assortment director needs a map of "how many products in each category and in each division" as one table: categories as rows, divisions as columns. A long list of category-division pairs is not something they will read.
tasks.goal: Build a pivot table over dim_product: rows are category, columns are division, values are the product count (product_id). Fill empty intersections with zero.
hints: pivot_table collapses several rows into one cell, and what exactly it does is set by aggfunc.
Products are to be counted, not summed: "count" fits (or "nunique", which gives the same on unique ids).
tasks.explain: pivot_table turns division into columns and counts the products at each intersection. Some intersections are empty by meaning: Pharma has no Beverages, so without fill_value=0 there would be NaN, and "no products" would look like "no data". The total is 29 FMCG products (Beverages 12, Dairy 6, Snacks 6, Home care 5) and 18 Pharma, all in the OTC category: 47 together.

tasks.title: The assortment map back to long format
tasks.brief: The "category by division" map has to be loaded into a BI system that accepts only long format: one category-division pair and one number per row.
tasks.goal: Reshape the table piv (category, FMCG, Pharma) back to long format: columns category, division, n_products.
hints: id_vars is the column that stays as is; the others turn into pairs of "column name → value".
var_name and value_name name the two new columns: the one with the former column names and the one with their values.
tasks.explain: melt is the reverse of pivot_table: 5 categories × 2 divisions give 10 rows, and zeros like Beverages × Pharma land in the result as ordinary values, because melt discards nothing. If the BI does not want zeros, a separate filter removes them: 5 real pairs remain. The pivot_table plus melt pair is the move between wide and long form that all of reshape works on.

tasks.title: How many customers have no rep
tasks.brief: Before reconciling the reports, the controller wants to know how many customers in the reference have no rep at all. Counting empty cells by eye in a table of 144 rows is not something they will do.
tasks.goal: Count the customers in dim_customer whose rep_id is missing.
hints: A method is needed that returns a boolean column: True where the value is missing.
sum() over a boolean column counts True as ones.
tasks.explain: The answer is 12, the very twelve that groupby on rep_id silently drops. isna() is the only reliable way to ask "is the value empty": the comparison rep_id == NaN finds nothing, because NaN does not equal anything, not even itself. Before any grouping on a column that may contain gaps it helps to count isna().sum() first, and then the losses are not a surprise.

traps.message: The result has all 144 customers, not 132: the comparison "!= None" is True for missing values too, because NaN does not equal anything, None included. The condition "a value is present" is written with the .notna() method.

tasks.title: Customers served by a distributor
tasks.brief: A mailing needs a list of customers attached to a distributor. For the rest (the distributors themselves in the reference) served_by_distributor_id is empty, and a comparison with emptiness through == or != will not work.
tasks.goal: Return columns customer_id and served_by_distributor_id for the customers in dim_customer whose served_by_distributor_id is filled in.
hints: The condition "a value is present" is a column method, the opposite of isna(); comparisons with NaN through == or != find nothing.
Rows and columns can be selected in one .loc[condition, [columns]].
tasks.explain: notna() picks 132 customers, and the 12 distributors with an empty field stay out of the frame. The mistake "!= None" or "== np.nan" is the classic one here: NaN equals nothing, so the condition drops nothing and the result is the same 144 rows. A side effect of gaps is visible too: the distributor id is stored as float (3.0 instead of 3), because an integer column cannot hold NaN.

traps.message: The total came out around 767,537 instead of 1,530,785, about half. With errors="coerce" every value with a comma ("392,44") quietly became a gap and dropped out of the sum, and there are 1,465 such values in the extract. Replace the comma with a dot first, then convert to a number.

tasks.title: Revenue written with a comma
tasks.brief: In staging_raw_sellout revenue is stored as text, and in some rows the decimal separator is a comma ("392,44"). Converting such text to a number directly fails with an error.
tasks.goal: Compute the sum of revenue in staging_raw_sellout: replace the comma with a dot, convert to a number and add up.
hints: The .str.replace(what, with) method replaces a substring in every value of the column at once.
The comma is what has to be replaced, so it goes in as the first argument, as text in quotes.
tasks.explain: A comma in the decimal part occurs in 1,465 of the 3,110 revenue values. Without the replacement astype(float) fails on the very first "392,44", while pd.to_numeric(errors="coerce") would quietly turn all 1,465 values into gaps, and the sum would come out too low with no warning at all. After the replacement every value goes into the sum except the 179 truly empty ones; the total is about 1.53 million.

traps.message: The answer is 3,110, every row of the extract, not 803. By default .str.contains reads the pattern as a regular expression, where a dot means "any character", so every date matched. To search for a literal dot, pass regex=False.

tasks.title: Dates with dots
tasks.brief: Dates in staging_raw_sellout are written in three formats: "2024-02-19", "11.03.2024" and "20/10/2025". Before converting them to one form the scale has to be clear: how many rows are written with a dot.
tasks.goal: Count the rows of staging_raw_sellout whose sale_date contains a dot.
hints: A substring in every value of the column is searched with .str.contains(...); sum() over the boolean column counts the matches.
By default .str.contains reads the pattern as a regular expression, where a dot means "any character"; to search for a literal dot, turn that off with regex=False.
tasks.explain: A dot is used in 803 of the 3,110 dates; a hyphen in 1,543, a slash in 764. Without regex=False the pattern "." would match any character and all 3,110 rows would count as found: the answer would look plausible and mean nothing. It is the same trap as in other string methods: special characters work as a pattern by default, not as letters.

tasks.title: Why duplicated() finds nothing
tasks.brief: The export from the accounting system shows two identical rows in a row, and the manager asks whether sales are doubled. The analyst checked the whole table with one line of code and got zero.
tasks.goal: Understand why checking the whole row finds none of the repeats that are visible by eye.
tasks.predictQuestion: staging_raw_sellout has 3,110 rows. Some are pairs that are identical in every column except the service number raw_id. What are a and b?

options.label: a = 0, b = 110: raw_id is different on every row, so while it is compared there are no repeats
options.why: duplicated() with no parameters compares the whole row, and raw_id (the export counter) makes every row unique even if a sale is recorded twice. Without that column the pairs become identical, and the method flags 110 repeated copies.

options.label: a = 110, b = 110: duplicated() ignores service numbers on its own
options.why: The method knows nothing about what the columns mean: it compares all of those it is given. A number that differs on every row makes comparing the whole row pointless, so a is zero.

options.label: a = 0, b = 0: there are actually no repeats in the export
options.why: There are repeats: 110 rows repeat the previous one in every column except raw_id. The zero in a only says that raw_id tells all rows apart, not that there are no duplicates.

options.label: a = 110, b = 0: without raw_id the table becomes more unique
options.why: The other way round: dropping a column that tells rows apart makes rows more alike. Pairs that differed only in raw_id become fully identical, and that is exactly when they are found.

hints: duplicated() compares rows across all the columns the table has at that moment.
A column that tells any two rows apart has to be taken out of the comparison, otherwise there is nothing for them to match on.
tasks.explain: The answer is a = 0 and b = 110. The raw_id column numbers the export rows one after another, so a copy of a sale has a number one higher than the original, and whole rows do not match. This is the most common cause of a silent "no repeats": no error, no warning, and the zero looks like good news. duplicated() flags only the repeated copies, the first one stays False, so 110 is the number of extra rows, not the number of rows in pairs (that is 220). The extra rows are 3.5% of the export.

tasks.title: How many extra rows are in the export
tasks.brief: A data manager noticed two identical rows in a row in staging_raw_sellout and asks how many such extra rows the whole export has. Comparing the whole row would say "zero", so the key is set explicitly: every column except the service raw_id.
tasks.goal: Count the rows of staging_raw_sellout that repeat an earlier row on a key of six columns.
hints: You need a method that answers "is this a repeat?" for each row and returns a boolean column, like isna().
sum() over a boolean column counts True as one. The method does not flag the first copy, only the repeated ones.
tasks.explain: The answer is 110: that many rows repeat an earlier one on the whole key. duplicated(subset=key) flags only repeated copies as True and leaves the first as False, so the sum is the number of extra rows, not the number of rows in pairs (that is 220). The subset parameter is the point here: without it raw_id would be part of the comparison, and the answer would be 0.

tasks.title: The order of working with repeats
tasks.brief: The export is accepted, but sales may be doubled in it. All five steps below are needed, yet deleting cannot be undone without reloading the table, so the order is not free.
tasks.goal: Arrange the steps so that each one builds on the result of the previous one.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do you work with repeats in an export?

items.label: Name the key: which columns make two rows the same sale (all except the service raw_id)
items.why: First, because both finding and deleting work on the key. Without it you are left comparing the whole row, where raw_id tells every pair apart and there are "no" repeats.

items.label: Look at the repeats by eye: select rows with keep=False and sort by the key so pairs sit side by side
items.why: Second: before deleting, make sure what was found really is one sale twice, not two different sales with similar values. A number will not show that, a pair of rows side by side shows it at once.

items.label: Estimate the scale: how many rows and how much revenue fall on the repeated copies
items.why: Third, and strictly before deleting: afterwards the extra rows cannot be found any more. The scale decides whether to clean the table yourself or send the export back to the source.

items.label: Remove the repeats: drop_duplicates on the same key, keeping the first copy
items.why: Fourth: this action cannot be undone for the working table. The key is the same as for finding and looking, otherwise something other than what you inspected gets deleted.

items.label: Check the count: there were 3,110 rows, 110 extra, exactly 3,000 should remain
items.why: Last: the check verifies the deletion itself. If the result is not 3,000, the key was different from the one used for finding, and it is better to catch that at once than in a report.

hints: One step defines what counts as a repeat at all. Without it the other four have nothing to work on.
You can only delete what you have already looked at and sized up. A check of the result is possible once there is something to check.
The estimate comes before the deletion: afterwards there are no repeated rows left in the table.
tasks.explain: The order rests on two rules. Decisions first, actions after: the key defines what a repeat is, and every later step depends on it. Reversible first, irreversible after: looking and estimating change nothing, deleting does. The final check uses the arithmetic from the third step: 3,110 minus 110 is 3,000. If the export arrives from the source with 3.7% of extra revenue, that is a reason to go back to the source, not only to clean a copy.

tasks.title: The export without repeats
tasks.brief: It was decided to clean the export rather than reissue it. You need a table in which every sale is recorded once: the first row of each pair stays, and calculations can go on without adjustments.
tasks.goal: How many rows of staging_raw_sellout remain if repeats on the six-column key are removed and the first copy is kept?
hints: You need a method that does not flag the repeats but removes them and returns the table without them.
The first copy is kept by default. The key goes in through the same subset parameter as when searching.
tasks.explain: 3,000 rows remain: 3,110 minus 110 repeated copies. By default drop_duplicates keeps the first copy of each group. Without subset the method compares whole rows, and raw_id makes each one unique: all 3,110 rows would come back with no error and no warning. A simple check "was, minus extras, equals remains" catches such a slip in a second.

traps.message: 3,110 rows remain, none was removed. Without subset drop_duplicates compares whole rows, and raw_id differs on every row, so no row is fully identical to another. The key has to be passed explicitly: subset=key, without raw_id.

tasks.title: How much revenue sits in the repeats
tasks.brief: A financial controller reconciles the export with the accounting system and asks how much revenue falls on repeated copies. If it is a lot, the export has to be reissued, not cleaned. Revenue in the table is text, and some values have a decimal comma.
tasks.goal: Calculate the revenue in the rows of staging_raw_sellout that repeat an earlier row in every column except raw_id. Round the result to 2 places.
hints: The key can be built as a list of all columns except raw_id. The repeated copies are selected by the boolean column duplicated(subset=key).
Revenue is text: before summing, replace the comma with a point and convert the column to numbers.
tasks.explain: The repeated copies carry 56,940.68 of the export's 1,530,784.50 total revenue, that is 3.7%. If they are not removed, the export's revenue is inflated by that amount. Three steps: a key without raw_id, converting text to numbers (the comma replacement is needed, otherwise to_numeric fails on values like "392,44"), then selecting with duplicated(subset=key) and summing. to_numeric turns empty revenue values into NaN, and sum() skips them.

traps.message: The result is 113,881.36, exactly twice as much. keep=False flags both rows of a pair, so the first one, the real sale, got counted as a "repeat". Only the second copy is extra, and by default (keep="first") only it is flagged.

tasks.title: Two overlapping conditions
tasks.brief: A buyer splits the catalog into price groups: from 100 ¥ mid, from 300 ¥ premium, the rest budget. The analyst wrote the two conditions in that order, and the resulting table had no premium products at all.
tasks.goal: Understand how np.select picks a label when a row passes several conditions at once.
tasks.predictQuestion: dim_product has 47 products: 32 of them cost 100 ¥ or more, and 11 of those 32 cost 300 ¥ or more. How many products get the label premium?

options.label: 0: a product above 300 ¥ already passed the first condition, and that one gives the label
options.why: np.select checks conditions in order and takes the label of the first one that fires. Any product from 300 ¥ also costs from 100 ¥, so it never reaches the second condition: all 32 products get mid and nobody gets premium.

options.label: 11: each condition takes its own products independently of the others
options.why: The conditions are not independent: the function looks at them in turn and stops at the first match. Independent selection would happen if the conditions did not overlap, but here "from 300" lies entirely inside "from 100".

options.label: 11, and mid gets 32: a product from 300 ¥ gets both labels
options.why: A row gets exactly one label, not a set. np.select returns a single array as long as the table, and each of its positions holds one value.

options.label: An error: the conditions overlap and NumPy refuses to compute
options.why: Overlapping conditions are not an error, they are the normal case: that is why the order of checking exists. There will be no warning, so the defect is visible only in the resulting table.

hints: np.select goes through the conditions left to right and, for each row, stops at the first one that is true.
Ask yourself whether any product passes the second condition without passing the first.
tasks.explain: The result is premium: 0, mid: 32, budget: 15. The condition "from 300 ¥" lies entirely inside "from 100 ¥", and placed second it cannot fire on any row. Swap the conditions and the result is premium: 11, mid: 21 (32 minus 11), budget: 15. No error, no warning: the missing label is visible only to someone who looks at the resulting table. In SQL, CASE WHEN does the same thing: branches are checked top to bottom, and the order decides.

tasks.title: Price groups of the catalog
tasks.brief: The buyer needs the catalog labeled: from 300 ¥ premium products, from 100 ¥ mid products, the rest budget. For a start it is enough to know how many products landed in each group.
tasks.goal: Label the products of dim_product into three price groups and count the products in each.
hints: You need a NumPy function that takes a list of conditions, a list of labels and a value for the remaining rows.
The narrow condition "from 300" comes first, the wide "from 100" after it.
tasks.explain: The result is budget: 15, mid: 21, premium: 11. The narrow condition comes first and takes the 11 most expensive products, the second takes the remaining 21 of those from 100 ¥, and the last 15 get the default. np.select returns an array of labels as long as the table, so it is wrapped in a pd.Series for counting. In SQL this is CASE WHEN list_price >= 300 THEN ... WHEN list_price >= 100 THEN ... ELSE ... END.

tasks.title: How to build np.select
tasks.brief: Rows have to be labeled by three rules with adjacent thresholds. All five steps are sensible, but if one is skipped or put in the wrong place, the labels come out wrong while the code runs without a single error.
tasks.goal: Arrange the steps so that the labels come out right and it is possible to check them.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do you build a labeling with np.select?

items.label: Write in words which label each group of rows should get
items.why: First: without the rules in words the conditions have to be invented along the way, and overlaps show up only in finished code. This is also where you see which groups lie inside others.

items.label: Arrange the conditions from the narrowest to the widest
items.why: Second, because np.select takes the first condition that fires. If a wide one stands before a narrow one, the narrow one never fires, and there is no error.

items.label: Decide which label rows that pass no condition get, and pass it as default
items.why: Third: this is also a decision about meaning, not a technical detail. Without default such rows get 0, and a label "0" appears in a column of text labels.

items.label: Call np.select and put the result into a column or a Series
items.why: Fourth, when the conditions and the default are settled. The call collects everything said above into an array of labels as long as the table.

items.label: Check the result: the counts by label add up to the table size and there is no label "0"
items.why: Last: the check compares the result with what was intended. A mismatched total or a "0" label shows that default was forgotten, and a missing group shows that the conditions are in the wrong order.

hints: Two steps decide what the code should do and come before the call itself. One step settles only the order inside the list.
There is nothing to check until the call has happened.
tasks.explain: The order is the same as for any code built on rules: rules first, then writing them down, then checking. Two np.select mistakes are silent: a condition that never fired because of the order, and a label "0" because of a missing default. Both are visible only in the resulting table, so the last step is not a formality: the counts by label must add up to the number of rows, and the set of labels must match the intended one.

tasks.title: Outlet segments by channel
tasks.brief: For the visit plan the outlets are split into three segments: chains, pharmacies and everything else. "Everything else" joins distributors, online and traditional retail, and they need no labels of their own.
tasks.goal: Label the outlets of dim_customer: modern_trade as chains, pharmacy as pharmacies, the rest as other. Count the outlets in each segment.
hints: The third argument of np.select is passed by name: it sets the label for rows that matched no condition.
Without it such rows get the number 0, not text.
tasks.explain: The result is other: 64, chains: 42, pharmacies: 38. other holds 12 distributors, 8 online stores and 44 traditional retail outlets. If default is not given, np.select puts in 0, and a string "0" appears among the text labels for the same 64 outlets: no error, just a strange segment living in the column. That is why default is always named, even when the conditions seem to cover everything.

traps.message: The result has a segment "0" with 64 outlets instead of other. When default is not set, np.select puts in the number 0, and it becomes the string "0" next to the text labels. There is no error, but a segment with that name tells nobody anything. Set default explicitly: default="other".

tasks.title: Promo and large sales apart
tasks.brief: A demand analyst wants to know what share of large sales is made by promotions. For that every row of fact_sellout must get one of three labels: promo, large regular or ordinary. A promo sale of 20 units or more must count as promo, not as large.
tasks.goal: Label fact_sellout: promo if the week has a promotion (promo_id is not empty); big if there is no promotion and 20 units or more were sold; regular in all other cases. Count the rows of each label.
hints: There are three labels, two conditions are needed, and the third label is given through default.
A promo sale of 20 units or more passes both conditions. The label promo must win, so its condition goes first.
A row with a promotion is one where promo_id is not missing, that is notna().
tasks.explain: The result is regular: 82,647, promo: 23,849, big: 11,953. The promo condition comes first, so the 2,765 sales that are both promo and 20 units or more went to promo. Swap the order and they would go to big: promo would shrink to 21,084 and big would grow to 14,718, that is, "large regular" sales would be a quarter higher than they really are. A narrow label with a special meaning always goes before a wide one.

traps.message: The result is promo: 21,084 and big: 14,718, but it should be 23,849 and 11,953. The condition "20 units or more" is first and takes all large sales, including 2,765 promo ones. They are counted as ordinary large ones, and big is inflated. The promo condition has to go first.

tasks.title: Where a value on an edge lands
tasks.brief: A sales manager splits weekly sales by size: up to 5 units small, up to 10 medium, the rest large. Two analysts wrote almost identical code, yet their resulting tables differ by thousands of rows.
tasks.goal: Understand which group a value equal to an edge falls into under different pd.cut settings.
tasks.predictQuestion: In fact_sellout, 9,249 rows were sold at exactly 5 units. Which group do they land in for a and for b?

options.label: a: small, b: medium
options.why: By default intervals are closed on the right: (0, 5], (5, 10], so the value 5 goes to the lower interval. With right=False the intervals are closed on the left: [0, 5), [5, 10), and the same value 5 becomes the first one in the middle interval.

options.label: a: medium, b: small
options.why: The other way round. If you remember that by default the right edge belongs to the interval, the value 5 stays in the lower one, and it is right=False that moves it up.

options.label: small in both cases: an edge always belongs to the lower group
options.why: It depends on the right parameter. It exists precisely to choose the side, and with right=False the edge goes to the upper group.

options.label: Neither: a value exactly on an edge belongs to no interval
options.why: The intervals join up: every edge belongs to one of the neighboring intervals, otherwise values on the edge would be lost. NaN goes to values outside all the edges, not on them.

hints: The edge between two intervals belongs to one of them. The question is which one.
The parameter right=True means the interval is closed on the right, that is, the right number is included.
tasks.explain: The result: in a the value 5 goes to small, in b to medium. That is why the tables differ: a has small 65,074, medium 22,830, large 30,545; b has small 55,825, medium 29,122, large 33,502. Both variants run with no error and no warning, so a condition like "up to 5 inclusive" or "from 5" has to be translated into right when the task is set, not guessed from the result.

tasks.title: Outlet size by revenue
tasks.brief: The head of sales splits outlets by total revenue over the whole period, and the thresholds are his own: under 100 thousand small, under 500 thousand medium, beyond that large. He needs to know how many outlets are in each group.
tasks.goal: Calculate each outlet's revenue in fact_sellout, split outlets by the thresholds 100,000 and 500,000 into small, medium and large, and count the outlets in each group.
hints: The edges are named by a person, not computed from the data. For such thresholds you need the function that takes a list of edges.
The other function of the same family splits by shares (quartiles) and takes a number of groups, not a list of edges.
tasks.explain: The result is large: 68, small: 41, medium: 23 (132 outlets in all). The business names the thresholds, so the groups come out of different sizes: most outlets are large. The lower edge 0 is below the minimum revenue (13,604) and the upper infinity accepts any value, so no outlet is lost. Compare with splitting by shares: pd.qcut(revenue, 3) would give 44 outlets in each group, but the thresholds would be random numbers nobody named.

tasks.title: How to split a number into groups
tasks.brief: Outlets have to be split into groups by revenue and the result shown to a manager. Each of the five steps is needed, but the order decides what ends up in the report: edges picked to fit the data, or edges that can be explained.
tasks.goal: Arrange the steps from getting to know the data to checking the result.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do you split a number into groups?

items.label: Look at the distribution: describe() or quantiles, the minimum and the maximum
items.why: First, because everything else depends on the shape of the distribution. One outlier shifts the mean and stretches the range, and without this look the edges are chosen blindly.

items.label: Decide where the edges come from: the business (cut) or shares (qcut)
items.why: Second: this is a decision about meaning. cut gives clear thresholds and groups of different sizes, qcut gives groups of equal size and unclear thresholds. The choice determines what the next step looks like.

items.label: Write the edges and group names, decide where a value on an edge goes and what to do about the minimum
items.why: Third: bins, labels and right are set together. A lower edge below the minimum and the side of closing decide whether some rows get lost and which group the boundary values land in.

items.label: Call pd.cut or pd.qcut and save the result into a column
items.why: Fourth, when the edges and labels are settled. The call only carries out decisions already made.

items.label: Check the result: the counts by group add up to the table size and there are no missing values (NaN)
items.why: Last: a missing value in the new column means a value outside the edges, that is, a lost row. A sum over the groups equal to the table size catches this in a second.

hints: There is a step after which the edges are chosen meaningfully, and before which they are chosen blindly.
The choice between cut and qcut comes before writing the edges themselves: qcut takes a number of groups instead of a list of edges.
tasks.explain: The order is the same as for any decision about data: look first, then decide, then carry out, then check. The choice between cut and qcut answers the question of what you want: clear edges or equal groups. Two mistakes are silent: a value on an edge goes to the wrong group, and the minimum becomes NaN. A sum over the groups checked against the table size catches the second at once, while the first is caught only by reading the condition of the task.

tasks.title: How much revenue is in each quarter of outlets
tasks.brief: The finance director wants to know how concentrated revenue is: split outlets into four groups equal in count and see how much each one brings.
tasks.goal: Split outlets by revenue into four groups Q1 to Q4 by shares (equal in the number of outlets) and calculate the revenue of each group, rounded to a whole number.
hints: The groups must be equal in the number of outlets, not in the width of the range. That is the function that takes a number of groups and finds the edges itself.
observed=True keeps only the intervals that actually occurred in the grouping and removes a pandas warning.
tasks.explain: The result is Q1: 1,403,142, Q2: 9,356,810, Q3: 23,302,412, Q4: 92,848,828. qcut splits 132 outlets into four groups of 33, and revenue is not split evenly between the groups at all: the top quarter brings 73% of all sales (92.8 of 126.9 million). Equal numbers of outlets in the groups do not mean equal revenue: this is what concentration looks like, and the average hides it.

tasks.title: Sale size: up to 5, up to 10, more
tasks.brief: A category manager splits weekly sales by units: small means up to 5 inclusive, medium from 6 to 10 inclusive, large more than 10. It matters to him that a sale of exactly 5 or 10 units lands in the right group and that no row goes missing.
tasks.goal: Split the sales of fact_sellout by the units column into small (up to 5 inclusive), medium (6 to 10) and large (more than 10), and count the rows in each group.
hints: The edges are named by a person, so you need pd.cut with a bins list and labels names.
The right edge is included in the interval by default, and the lower edge must be below the smallest sale, otherwise it falls into no interval.
tasks.explain: The result is small: 65,074, medium: 22,830, large: 30,545, 118,449 rows in all. The intervals are (0, 5], (5, 10], (10, infinity): the value 5 stays in small, the value 10 in medium. The lower edge 0 is below the minimum (1), so sales of one unit are not lost. Two mistakes here are silent: the side of closing moves boundary values into the neighboring group, and a lower edge of 1 turns every sale of one unit into NaN, which value_counts does not show.

traps.message: The result is small: 55,825, medium: 29,122, large: 33,502. The intervals are now closed on the left, and sales of exactly 5 units moved from small to medium, and of 10 units from medium to large. The condition "up to 5 inclusive" requires intervals closed on the right: that is the default behavior (right=True).

small has 50,745 rows instead of 65,074: 14,329 sales of one unit are lost. The interval (1, 5] does not include its lower edge, so the value 1 became NaN, and value_counts does not show missing values. Take the lower edge below the minimum (here 0) or add include_lowest=True.

tasks.title: The upper edge by the IQR rule
tasks.brief: A demand analyst wants to find unusually large rows in weekly sales. He took the Tukey rule: anything above the third quartile by more than one and a half interquartile ranges counts as unusual.
tasks.goal: Calculate the upper edge by the IQR rule and understand what it marks.
tasks.predictQuestion: The first quartile of units is 3 and the third is 11. What is upper equal to?

options.why: The interquartile range IQR = 11 − 3 = 8. One and a half ranges is 12, and the edge lies 12 above the third quartile: 11 + 12 = 23. Anything sold above 23 units a week counts as unusually large.

options.label: 19: 11 + (11 − 3), the third quartile plus one range
options.why: The factor 1.5 is forgotten. One and a half ranges shift the edge by 12, not by 8. A rule with a factor of 1 would flag noticeably more ordinary values.
That is only the offset from the third quartile. The edge is measured from the quartile itself: q3 has to be added to the 12.

options.label: 14: 3 + 11, the sum of the quartiles
options.why: The sum of the quartiles is not an edge. The formula takes the distance between them (the range) and lays it off upward from the third quartile.

hints: IQR is the difference between the third and the first quartile, that is, the width of the middle half of the data.
The edge is laid off upward from the third quartile, not from zero and not from the median.
tasks.explain: The result is upper = 23. Above this edge lie 10,926 rows out of 118,449, that is 9.2%. It matters that the IQR rule answers only "is the value unusually large", not "is it an error": the flagged rows have to be looked at, not thrown out. They carry 38.2% of all units sold, so deleting them would noticeably change the totals.

tasks.title: How many rows are above the edge
tasks.brief: Before any talk of outliers you need the scale: how many rows of weekly sales are above the Tukey edge. It decides whether to look at them one by one or in groups.
tasks.goal: Count the rows of fact_sellout whose units are above q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
hints: You need the same method as in the line above: it takes a share from 0 to 1 and returns the value below which that share of the rows lies.
The third quartile is the share 0.75.
tasks.explain: The result is 10,926 rows, 9.2% of the table. quantile(0.25) gives 3, quantile(0.75) gives 11, the edge is 11 + 1.5 × 8 = 23. The comparison u > upper returns a boolean column, and sum() counts the True values. The rows stay in place: so far it is only a flag, not a deletion.

tasks.title: What to do with unusually large values
tasks.brief: Weekly sales have rows that stand far out upward. The manager asks to "remove the outliers so the average does not lie". Each of the five steps is sensible, but the order separates careful analysis from losing real data.
tasks.goal: Arrange the steps so that the decision to exclude rests on what you have seen.
tasks.orderQuestion: In what order do you work with unusually large values?

items.label: Calculate the edge by the IQR rule: the quartiles and the upper threshold
items.why: First: without an edge there is no definition of "unusually large" and nothing to discuss. This is also where you decide within which group the edge is calculated.

items.label: Mark values above the edge in a separate flag column, keep the rows
items.why: Second: a flag changes nothing in the data and is undone with one line. Deleting is irreversible, and the decision has not been made yet.

items.label: Look at what was marked: which products, which weeks, whether there is a promotion
items.why: Third: the rule answers only "is it unusually large". Whether it is an error or a real event is visible only from the content of the marked rows.

items.label: Decide by cause: fix or remove an error, keep and explain an event
items.why: Fourth: the decision rests on what was seen. Promotions and stock-ups are real sales, and deleting them understates the total.

items.label: Record what was excluded and why, and only then recalculate the metric
items.why: Last: an exclusion without a record cannot be checked or repeated. A metric recalculated before the decision gets fitted to the wanted answer.

hints: One step turns the edge into a visible result without changing the data. It comes before all the steps that decide something.
You can decide whether to keep or remove a value only after finding out what caused it.
tasks.explain: The order rests on two rules: reversible first, irreversible after, and understand first, decide after. The IQR rule gives suspects, not culprits. In this data the largest rows (232, 194 and 185 units) are all promotions: they are real sales, and "removing the outliers" would understate demand exactly where it is highest.

tasks.title: An edge per product, not per table
tasks.brief: A common edge mostly marks rows of big products: their ordinary sales are larger too. To find what is unusual for the product itself, the edge has to be computed inside each product.
tasks.goal: Count the rows of fact_sellout whose units are above q3 + 1.5 × IQR, computed separately for the product_id of that row.
hints: You need the groupby method that returns a group value for every row, a column as long as the table.
It is already in the line above, for the first quartile.
tasks.explain: The result is 7,250 rows against 10,926 with a common edge. transform("quantile", 0.75) puts the third quartile of its product into every row, so each product has its own edge. The common edge marks whole products: four products (2, 1, 7 and 24) account for 30% of all marked rows because their ordinary sales are larger. An edge per product marks what is unusual for the product itself.

tasks.title: The share of promotions among unusual sales of a product
tasks.brief: A demand analyst suspects that unusually large sales of a product are promotions. Easy to check: compare the share of promo weeks among such sales with the share of promotions in the whole table (it is 20.1%).
tasks.goal: Mark the rows of fact_sellout whose units are above q3 + 1.5 × IQR inside their product_id, and output the share of promo rows (promo_id is not empty) among the marked ones, in percent, rounded to 1 place.
hints: The edge per product comes from groupby("product_id")["units"].transform("quantile", share): you need the first and the third quartile.
The mean of a boolean column is the share. Promo rows are those where promo_id is not missing.
tasks.explain: The result is 39.2%: of the 7,250 marked rows 2,840 are promotions, while promotions make up 20.1% of the whole table. Sales unusually large for their product are twice as often promotions, and that is an event, not an error. An edge over the whole table does not see this link: among its 10,926 rows promotions are exactly 20.1%, same as everywhere, because it marks big products, not unusual weeks. The takeaway for work: a flag tells you where to look, and these rows must not be deleted.

traps.message: The result is 20.1%, the same as promotions in the whole table. The edge was computed over the whole table and marked big products as a whole, not unusual weeks: promotions among them are as common as anywhere, and the link vanished. The edge has to be computed inside a product: groupby("product_id") and transform("quantile", ...).
